notes.1: The solution to this problem required the use of the conservation of momentum law. Whilst this was frequently applied correctly, the momentum before the collision was quite often calculated as (0.4 × 2.5 + 0.5 × 1.5) = 1.75 instead of (0.4 × 2.5 – 0.5 × 1.5) = 0.25. The condition that ‘the speed of Q is twice the speed of P’ was sometimes misinterpreted and misapplied by candidates. To obtain a second solution candidates needed to recognise that after the collision the particles either travelled in the same direction with momentum (0.4v + 0.5(2v)) or in opposite directions (– 0.4v + 0.5(2v)). Some solutions concluded with a negative velocity rather than the speed of particle P. Final answers were occasionally seen as 0.18ms–1 and 0.42ms–1 rather than the three significant figure values expected. A few candidates considered conservation of energy rather than conservation of momentum.
notes.2a: The majority of candidates applied Newton’s Second Law and solved the resulting equation accurately. Occasionally the resistance force was omitted, thus = 0.25m leading to m = 150kg. In other solutions the resistance appeared to be in the same direction as the driving force, thus +20 = 0.25m leading to m = 230kg following the sign error.

notes.3: This question was well attempted by nearly all candidates who frequently resolved the forces and solved the resulting simultaneous equations accurately. Final answers of F = 16.6 and θ = 65.8 instead of F = 16.5 and θ = 65.7 were seen following premature approximations such as Fsinθ = 15.1 or tanθ = 2.22. Other errors included sign errors or the use of sine instead of cosine or cosine instead of sine when resolving or when substituting for sin α, sinβ, cos α or cosβ. notes.4a: The great majority of candidates applied s = ut + at2 appropriately to obtain the given result u = 22. A few mistakenly assumed a greatest height of 24m with velocity v = 0 and applied v2 = u2 + 2as to obtain u = 480 =22 approximately.
notes.4b: This part was found to be more challenging and produced a variety of attempted methods. The question involved the use of constant acceleration formulae usually in two stages to find h. It was essential to realise that 3.6 seconds was the time spent above h m with 1.8 seconds rising and 1.8 seconds falling. It was common to see s = ut – gt2 applied with u = 22 and t = 3.6 leading mistakenly to s = 14.4, the displacement from the ground after 3.6 s rather than h. Many candidates were able to find the greatest height reached (24.2m) or the time taken to reach it (2.2 s), but could not always progress further to find h. One possible method was to find the time taken 2.2–  s to reach h m and then apply s = ut – gt2. Alternatively, the distance above h m could be found using s = 0 t + gt2 with t = 1.8 s. Those who used this method sometimes forgot to subtract the distance above h m from the greatest height to find h.
notes.5a: The most common method of solution was to form and solve a work/energy equation for the whole system. In forming the expected equation PE loss + WD by the engine = KE gain, the common errors were to omit one of the three terms or to combine the terms with an incorrect sign or both. For example, 1900g × s × sin 5 = × 1900 × (302 – 202) + 150000, s = 377 (sign error) or 150000 = 1900g × s × sin 5, s = 90.6 (no kinetic energy and a sign error). Occasionally there was a repeated 1900g sin 5 × s if it was not realised that the work done by the component of weight is the potential energy loss. Those who formed a work/energy equation in terms of h (the change in height) needed to apply to find the distance required. Those who attempted work/energy equations for either the car or the trailer separately needed to realise that both equations were necessary since this method involved two unknowns: the tension in the tow-bar as well as the length of the hill.
notes.5b: The most straightforward solutions used v2 = u2 + 2as to find the acceleration down the hill and then applied F = ma to the trailer. Those who involved either the car or the whole system in the solution frequently either overlooked the driving force or assumed it to be 150000÷200 with the work done by the engine unchanged from part (a). Thus it was common to see the solution of erroneous simultaneous equations such as 1400gsin5–T =1400a and T +500gsin5–100=500aor 750+1400gsin5–T =1400a and T +500gsin5–100=500a. Some candidates attempted a longer solution using a work/energy equation for the system in order to find the actual driving force before attempting simultaneous equations. Those who attempted this method either for the system or for the car alone, sometimes confused the tension and the driving force without realising that both were acting on the car. A clear and complete force diagram may have been helpful in assessing the forces acting on the car, the trailer and the system as a whole.

notes.7a: This was a ‘show that’ question with an exact answer given and requiring clear and exact working. Since sinθ was given as an exact value, it was possible to find cosθ without calculating and using an approximate value (16.3o) for the angle θ. The solution involved resolving parallel and perpendicular to the plane and applying F = μR. Both F (the frictional force) and R (the normal reaction) combined a component of 0.3g N with a component of the 4 N force. A common error was to omit one component when resolving, e.g. R = 3cosθ. The clearest solutions showed the substitutions for sinθ and cosθ using exact values either before or after the application of F = μR.
notes.7b: The application of Newton’s Second Law was usually recognised to be the method of solution. The equation of motion for particle P should have contained the component of weight and the frictional force acting down the plane, and the 4 N force acting up the plane. One common error was to assume that the frictional force was unchanged by the new direction of the 4 N force. Thus 4 – 3sin θ – 3 = 0.3a, a = 0.533 was seen repeatedly, with μR = 3 instead of μR =0.75 × 3cosθ. Other solutions omitted either the weight component 4 – 0.75 × 3cosθ = 0.3a, a = 6.13 or omitted the frictional force 4 – 3sin θ = 0.3a, a = 10.5.
notes.7c: This was found to be a more challenging question which was not always attempted. The problem involved two stages of motion, before and after the removal of the 4 N force. Having calculated the initial acceleration of the particle in part (b), the ‘suvat’ formulae could be used to find the distance moved up the plane whilst accelerating, and the speed of particle P when the 4 N force was removed. The main errors arose when calculating the acceleration after the removal of the 4 N force. This required another application of F = ma. The acceleration was sometimes stated erroneously as a = –gsinθ or a = –g or calculated with the component of weight and the frictional force acting in opposite directions, or with the frictional force still including the 4 N force. A final application of v2 = u2 + 2as enabled the distance whilst decelerating to be calculated. In some cases, the particle appeared to have an acceleration to v = 0 rather than a deceleration to v = 0. MATHEMATICS
notes.key_messages: The question paper contains a statement in the rubric on the front cover that ‘no marks will be given for unsupported answers from a calculator.’ This means that clear working must be shown to justify solutions, particularly in syllabus items such as quadratic equations and trigonometric equations. In the case of quadratic equations, for example, it would be necessary to show factorisation, use of the quadratic formula or completing the square as stated in the syllabus. Using calculators to solve equations and writing down only the solution is not sufficient for certain marks to be awarded. It is also insufficient to quote only the formula:
notes.general_comments: General comments Some very good responses were seen but the paper proved very challenging for many candidates. In AS and A Level Mathematics papers the knowledge and use of basic algebraic and trigonometric methods from IGCSE or O Level is expected, as stated in the syllabus. Comments on specific questions Many candidates successfully found the equation of the curve, including evaluating the constant of integration. A significant number of candidates omitted the constant. Weaker responses used differentiation instead of integration.
